narrative:
# Cross‑Currents In Growth: Semis Melt Up, Software Unwinds, Banks Stabilize

The past week delivered an unusually sharp divergence across our watchlist, with high‑beta software and security selling off hard at the same time that semiconductors, hyperscalers, and select cyclicals staged powerful rallies.
Semiconductors led decisively, with names like Astera Labs, Intel, Marvell, Broadcom, and several test and measurement players advancing between roughly 18% and 27% over the week, while memory, storage, and data‑center infrastructure followed suit.
At the other end of the spectrum, application software, cloud infrastructure, and cybersecurity saw broad‑based drawdowns, with numerous franchises down between mid‑teens and low‑thirties percent over just a few sessions, despite a relatively benign near‑term fundamental news flow.
This combination of factor‑driven rotation, position de‑risking in crowded software longs, and renewed enthusiasm for semis and capex beneficiaries is redefining leadership into mid‑year and sets up a more nuanced opportunity set, particularly for investors willing to lean against extremes in both directions.

## Market Overview

The dominant feature of the week was a violent style and sector rotation rather than a uniform macro‑driven risk‑on or risk‑off move.
Across our universe, the dispersion in one‑week returns is extreme: Fastly declined about 31.1% while Astera Labs gained 27.2%, Intel rallied 23.8%, and Sandisk, SiTime, and Marvell were all up roughly 20% or more.
This type of spread over a short horizon rarely reflects company‑specific news alone and instead signals a shift in market preferences within growth: away from long‑duration, still‑loss‑making or richly valued software compounders and toward more tangible beneficiaries of the current AI and data‑center investment cycle.
Within our large‑cap growth bellwethers, the picture is more balanced: Amazon advanced 13.6% on the week and Meta gained 9.6%, while Alphabet rose 7.2%; these moves underscore that mega‑cap platforms remain relative safe havens inside the growth complex, even as smaller software peers sold off.

From a style perspective, quality and profitability screens appear to be reasserting themselves after a period in which investors were willing to pay elevated multiples for secular growth in software, security, and vertical applications.
Enterprise software broadly de‑rated, with names like HubSpot, ServiceNow, Intuit, Atlassian, Workday, Asana, and several others all falling between the low‑teens and just over 21% for the week.
Cybersecurity was similarly weak, with Okta down 21.5%, and a cluster of high‑quality but fully valued names like Zscaler, Rubrik, Qualys, SentinelOne, and Varonis all falling around the low‑ to mid‑teens.
Meanwhile, the banks, card issuers, and diversified financials were generally constructive: Bank of America and LPL Financial both advanced 6.4%, Capital One gained 6.1%, Wells Fargo climbed 6.0%, Synchrony rose 5.8%, Goldman Sachs was up 5.2%, and Morgan Stanley added 7.1%, reinforcing the view that the credit cycle remains manageable and interest‑sensitive financials remain investable.

The divergence within technology subsectors is particularly striking.
Software infrastructure names such as Fastly, Akamai, Cloudflare, Snowflake, Samsara, Procore, Amplitude, and UiPath collectively experienced one‑week drawdowns ranging from roughly 14% to more than 31%, despite their centrality to secular themes like cloud migration, observability, and applied AI.
Application software fared no better, with Guidewire, HubSpot, ServiceNow, Intuit, BlackLine, Atlassian, Workday, and Asana each giving back between about 14% and 22%.
In contrast, the semiconductor cohort delivered broad and robust gains: Astera Labs, Intel, Sandisk, SiTime, Marvell, Onto Innovation, Teradyne, and Broadcom rallied between 18% and 27%, reflecting renewed confidence in the durability of the AI hardware cycle and, in several cases, short‑covering from increasingly crowded underweight positions.

The relative calm in defensives compared with the turbulence in software also stands out.
Consumer staples on our list moved mostly higher: McCormick and Constellation Brands each gained 9.9%, Unilever advanced 5.2%, and Keurig Dr Pepper rose 5.0%.
Select industrials and power‑related names such as Comfort Systems USA, GE Vernova, Caterpillar, CNH Industrial, Valmont, Generac, and BWX Technologies advanced between high single digits and low‑ to mid‑teens, aligning with the notion that energy transition and infrastructure spend remain medium‑term support pillars.
Metals and materials were mixed, though copper‑levered Freeport‑McMoRan climbed 10.5%, Nucor rose 7.9%, Kaiser Aluminum gained 8.4%, and Newmont advanced 6.0%, suggesting that investors still value real‑asset exposure as a hedge within portfolios.

The absence of imminent earnings catalysts for our watchlist over the next two weeks further accentuates the role of positioning and macro narrative rather than idiosyncratic news.
With no watchlist constituents set to report in the coming fortnight, the market’s repricing of software relative to semis appears driven by valuation, crowding, and factor flows rather than fresh guidance resets.
That increases the risk that investors over‑extrapolate short‑term factor moves into structural conclusions, especially in high‑quality franchises whose medium‑term fundamentals remain intact.
For buy‑side portfolios, this creates both risk and opportunity: the risk of being caught on the wrong side of factor rotations, and the opportunity to upgrade portfolio quality by recycling capital from names that have become more fully valued into those where the drawdown has refreshed prospective returns.

## Sector Leadership & Rotation

This week’s leadership is most easily understood as a continuation and intensification of a rotation within growth rather than a simple growth‑versus‑value regime change.
Semiconductors sit at the epicenter of that rotation.
Astera Labs rallied 27.2% on the week and 19.5% over the month, while Intel advanced 23.8% over the week and 30.0% over the month, signaling a strong re‑rating as investors reassess both companies’ roles in the AI and high‑bandwidth connectivity stack.
Marvell rose 20.0% for the week and 42.1% for the month, Broadcom gained 18.1% on the week and 8.8% over the month, SiTime climbed 21.1% weekly and 19.8% monthly, and Onto Innovation and Teradyne gained around 19.3% and 18.9% respectively.
These moves reflect both cyclical tailwinds as inventory digestion abates and structural tailwinds as AI compute requirements accelerate demand for leading‑edge silicon, memory, packaging, and test.

Memory and storage‑linked names also joined the rally.
Sandisk advanced 21.4% for the week and 30.0% for the month, while Seagate rose 17.2% weekly and 30.4% monthly and Western Digital climbed 16.4% weekly and 27.8% monthly.
Micron gained 14.8% on the week and is modestly positive over the month.
These performances suggest that the market increasingly views the memory cycle as early‑ to mid‑upturn, with AI‑driven demand for high‑bandwidth memory and enterprise storage offsetting concerns over traditional PC and handset end markets.
Importantly, these storage and memory moves also feed into the broader AI infrastructure narrative, as hyperscaler and enterprise data‑center capex keeps shifting from pure compute toward a more balanced stack that includes networking, storage, and cooling.

Cloud infrastructure, by contrast, was on the receiving end of risk‑off flows despite its strategic importance.
Fastly dropped 31.1% over the week and 4.1% over the month, Akamai declined 22.6% weekly and 14.2% monthly, Cloudflare fell 21.1% weekly and 21.6% monthly, and Snowflake lost 20.2% for the week and 32.5% for the month.
Samsara was down 19.9% over the week and 19.4% over the month, Procore declined 18.7% weekly and 15.9% monthly, Amplitude fell 18.0% weekly and 26.6% monthly, while UiPath dropped 16.6% over the week and 24.2% over the month.
These moves are too correlated and broad‑based to be purely idiosyncratic; they instead reflect a de‑rating of high‑multiple software tied to digital transformation and observability themes, especially those with still‑elevated sales and marketing expense or unproven operating leverage.

Application software showed a similar pattern.
Guidewire declined 21.8% for the week and 25.5% over the month, HubSpot fell 21.4% weekly and 25.8% monthly, ServiceNow dropped 18.6% weekly and 28.2% monthly, and Intuit lost 16.9% for the week and 20.3% for the month.
BlackLine declined 16.5% weekly and 16.2% monthly, Atlassian fell 16.3% weekly and 24.2% monthly, Workday slid 14.9% weekly and 18.4% monthly, and Asana decreased 14.3% for the week and 22.6% over the month.
The common thread is a combination of premium valuations, slowing incremental growth in certain sub‑segments, and a growing investor preference for businesses with clear near‑term cash‑flow scalability, especially as discount‑rate narratives remain in flux.

Cybersecurity, which had been a notable outperformer over the past couple of years, also came under sustained pressure.
Okta declined 21.5% for the week and 22.2% over the month, while Rubrik fell 14.8% weekly and 23.8% monthly and Zscaler declined 14.8% weekly and 23.2% monthly.
Qualys dropped 13.8% for the week and 21.2% for the month, with SentinelOne and Varonis each down 10.4% weekly and mid‑teens percentages monthly; Check Point and Tenable both fell 8.8% over the week, with double‑digit percentage declines over the month.
This broad step down reflects concerns about budget prioritization, platform consolidation, and competitive intensity as larger vendors push integrated offerings and buyers seek to rationalize security tool sprawl.
Yet the selloff has likely also overshot fundamentals in several names, setting up a more favorable entry point for investors with a twelve‑ to twenty‑four‑month horizon.

Against this backdrop, hyperscale platforms and AI beneficiaries maintain leadership.
Nvidia advanced 6.3% for the week and 1.4% for the month, which is notable given the already large gains over preceding quarters and signals that investors remain comfortable underwriting further data‑center GPU demand.
Amazon gained 13.6% weekly and 12.1% monthly, supported by improving retail margins and an increasingly constructive narrative around AWS’s AI positioning.
Meta rose 9.6% on the week despite being slightly negative over the month, while Alphabet added 7.2% weekly and 2.4% monthly.
The relative resilience of these mega‑caps, especially in a week marked by sharp software drawdowns, underscores their role as core positions for growth investors and as vehicles for AI exposure with diversified earnings streams.

Financials, while not in outright leadership compared with the hottest semis, are firmly in the constructive camp.
Bank of America’s 6.4% weekly and 8.3% monthly gains, Wells Fargo’s 6.0% weekly and 11.1% monthly performance, and JPMorgan’s 5.2% weekly and 7.8% monthly rise all point to sustained confidence in large U.S. banks’ balance sheets and earnings power.
Capital One and Synchrony, both more exposed to consumer credit, gained 6.1% and 5.8% over the week and around 6.0% and 11.0% over the month respectively, implying that investors see consumer credit normalization as manageable.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, with weekly gains of 5.2% and 7.1% and monthly gains around 10.2% and 10.4% respectively, benefited from stronger capital markets activity and the prospect of gradually improving advisory pipelines.

Within consumer, rotation is more nuanced.
Digital commerce names such as Wix and Shopify suffered, with Wix declining 20.5% weekly and 27.6% monthly and Shopify down 6.3% weekly and 14.5% monthly.
The Trade Desk in digital advertising fell 8.9% weekly and 26.4% monthly, while ad‑tech names like Braze and Klaviyo saw weekly declines of 19.9% and 14.3% respectively.
In contrast, PVH rallied 17.7% weekly and 48.7% over the month, highlighting that select branded apparel retailers can still deliver strong equity performance when execution and valuation align.
McCormick and Constellation Brands, both consumer staples, gained 9.9% for the week; Unilever rose 5.2% despite being down over the month, and Keurig Dr Pepper gained 5.0%, reinforcing the defensive appeal of staples amid volatility elsewhere.

Energy and industrials also contributed positively to sector rotation.
Corning, a key specialty materials supplier into communications and display markets, gained 15.8% weekly and 30.0% monthly, reflecting its leverage to data‑center and network build‑outs.
Comfort Systems USA advanced 12.4% weekly and 13.2% monthly, GE Vernova increased 10.3% weekly and 16.9% monthly, and Caterpillar rose 10.2% weekly and 11.7% monthly, all consistent with ongoing infrastructure, power, and data‑center construction themes.
Freeport‑McMoRan’s 10.5% weekly and 10.2% monthly gains, along with an 8.4% weekly and 11.8% monthly rise at Kaiser Aluminum and a 7.9% weekly and 8.3% monthly gain at Nucor, speak to investors’ desire for exposure to industrial metals as both a cyclical and secular play.

## Top Movers & Earnings Recap

With no watchlist earnings on the calendar for the next two weeks, this week’s top movers were primarily driven by positioning, valuation, and thematic flows rather than fresh quarterly numbers or guidance changes.
The most dramatic downside move was Fastly, which declined 31.1% for the week and is now down 4.1% over the month.
Fastly sits at the nexus of content delivery and edge compute, a space that should benefit from rising AI inference at the edge and richer media consumption, yet the stock’s drawdown suggests a reset in expectations around the pace of margin expansion and competitive dynamics.
Given the lack of a new earnings print this week, the selloff likely reflects a combination of factor‑driven selling in unprofitable software and mounting concerns about the timeline for achieving durable free‑cash‑flow positive growth.

Other notable downside movers include Akamai, down 22.6% for the week and 14.2% for the month, and Cloudflare, down 21.1% weekly and 21.6% monthly.
Both names share exposure to security and edge infrastructure, but their factor profiles differ; Cloudflare has been treated as a pure high‑growth multiple stock, while Akamai is viewed as a more mature, cash‑generative infrastructure provider.
The fact that both fell sharply suggests that investors are re‑rating the entire edge and web security sub‑complex, potentially pricing in slower usage growth and more intense competition.
Snowflake’s 20.2% weekly and 32.5% monthly decline is similarly instructive; the company remains a central data‑platform player, yet the stock now embeds a lower growth‑duration premium than it did even a month ago.

On the application software side, HubSpot’s 21.4% weekly and 25.8% monthly decline stands out.
HubSpot has been one of the most admired mid‑cap software franchises, with strong product velocity in CRM and marketing automation.
The recent drawdown likely reflects a combination of elevated starting valuations, some investor fatigue after a long stretch of outperformance, and concerns that AI‑enabled tools could compress pricing in certain segments of the marketing technology stack.
Guidewire’s 21.8% weekly and 25.5% monthly decline and ServiceNow’s 18.6% weekly and 28.2% monthly drop tell a similar story: even high‑quality, mission‑critical software is not immune when the market re‑prices the entire software complex.

Okta’s 21.5% weekly and 22.2% monthly decline makes it one of the weakest performers in cybersecurity.
The identity category remains structurally important, but Okta has navigated both integration challenges and competitive noise.
This week’s move, in the absence of a new earnings report, underscores how quickly sentiment can swing when investors re‑focus on execution risk and the potential for platform consolidation.
Other security names like Rubrik and Zscaler, both down 14.8% for the week, and Qualys, SentinelOne, Varonis, Check Point, and Tenable, down between about 8.8% and 13.8%, illustrate that the market is applying a broad discount to the group.
The more mature, cash‑generative names may prove more resilient over time, but in the near term, factor flows dominate.

On the positive side, the semiconductors provided a long list of top weekly gainers.
Astera Labs’ 27.2% weekly and 19.5% monthly rise, Intel’s 23.8% weekly and 30.0% monthly move, and Marvell’s 20.0% weekly and 42.1% monthly rally all point to renewed enthusiasm for data‑center and networking‑heavy silicon.
Sandisk’s 21.4% weekly and 30.0% monthly performance and SiTime’s 21.1% weekly and 19.8% monthly gains highlight that the market is not only rewarding compute‑centric chips but also timing and storage components that are critical to the broader infrastructure.
Onto Innovation’s 19.3% weekly and 33.4% monthly rise and Teradyne’s 18.9% weekly and 21.9% monthly gain underscore the leverage of test and inspection vendors to foundry and packaging utilization.

Outside semis, PVH’s 17.7% weekly and 48.7% monthly performance is among the strongest on our list.
Such a move in a branded apparel name suggests that the company has either delivered or is expected to deliver strong execution on product and inventory, as well as effective cost control.
Seagate’s 17.2% weekly and 30.4% monthly rise and Western Digital’s 16.4% weekly and 27.8% monthly move highlight how quickly sentiment can shift in storage when investors grow comfortable with the trajectory of bit demand and pricing.
Arista Networks’ 16.3% weekly and 6.6% monthly gain and Vertiv’s 12.9% weekly and 10.0% monthly performance further confirm the market’s appetite for data‑center networking and power infrastructure, both direct beneficiaries of rising AI workloads.

On the large‑cap technology and consumer internet front, Amazon’s 13.6% weekly and 12.1% monthly gain is a noteworthy outlier on the upside.
The stock’s move reflects mounting evidence of improved profitability in the core retail business and an increasingly favorable narrative around AWS’s ability to monetize generative AI services on top of its existing cloud installed base.
Meta’s 9.6% weekly gain, despite being modestly down over the month, suggests that markets remain comfortable with the balance between its heavy AI infrastructure spending and the monetization of its core advertising franchises.
Alphabet’s 7.2% weekly and 2.4% monthly rise keeps it in the group of stable AI‑levered mega‑caps.
These names continue to act as relative shelters within growth, especially in weeks when mid‑cap software and security experience abrupt de‑ratings.

Financials’ performance, while less headline‑grabbing than semis, is crucial from a portfolio‑stability standpoint.
Bank of America’s 6.4% weekly and 8.3% monthly gain, Wells Fargo’s 6.0% weekly and 11.1% monthly performance, JPMorgan’s 5.2% weekly and 7.8% monthly move, and Goldman Sachs’s 5.2% weekly and 10.2% monthly advance collectively signal that the market remains confident in the earnings trajectory of large U.S. banks and investment banks.
Morgan Stanley’s 7.1% weekly and 10.4% monthly gain, along with LPL Financial’s 6.4% weekly and 3.2% monthly move and Synchrony’s 5.8% weekly and 11.0% monthly rise, support the notion that capital markets and consumer credit concerns are moderating relative to earlier in the cycle.

## Macro & Rates Environment

While this week’s dispersion across our watchlist is striking, it is notable that it occurred without an accompanying slate of company‑level earnings and against a macro backdrop that has been relatively stable on a week‑over‑week basis.
The macro environment remains characterized by a central‑bank stance that is data‑dependent and cautious, with policymakers balancing the need to maintain inflation progress against the risk of overtightening.
Recent macro data have been mixed rather than extreme in either direction, offering neither a clear green light nor a decisive red flag for risk assets.
As such, equity markets have increasingly been driven by micro and thematic narratives—AI, data‑center capex, and software valuation resets—rather than by broad index‑level reactions to macro surprises.

Within fixed income, yield curves remain shaped by expectations of a gradual path for policy rather than an abrupt pivot.
Although exact yield levels have moved day‑to‑day, the overarching narrative is that the front end is anchored by policy expectations, while the long end reflects both term premia and a modest growth premium.
For equities, that translates into a discount‑rate environment that neither strongly supports multiple expansion nor forces a wholesale de‑rating, but instead amplifies differentiation between cash‑generative, near‑term earners and long‑duration growth stories.
This helps explain why semis and financials, which are seen as closer to the current cash‑flow cycle, outperformed, while more distant‑cash‑flow sectors like early‑stage software sold off.

Inflation dynamics continue to evolve in a direction that is broadly supportive but not yet conclusive.
Headline and core readings over recent months have suggested that disinflation is continuing, but there have been enough upside and downside surprises to keep investors cautious.
In this context, sticky services inflation, particularly in categories like shelter and certain labor‑intensive services, remains in focus.
For corporate earnings, this backdrop means continued wage and input‑cost pressure in labor‑heavy industries, offset by the potential for price discipline where companies have strong competitive positions.

For technology and software, the macro channel works primarily through enterprise IT budgets and the cost of capital.
So far, CIO surveys and reported results earlier in the quarter have pointed to stable but scrutinized IT spending, with prioritization of mission‑critical and ROI‑accretive projects, including AI, security, and core infrastructure.
The recent software drawdown, in our view, is therefore more about valuation, crowding, and a re‑rating after a strong multi‑quarter run than about an abrupt change in underlying demand.
Semiconductors, on the other hand, sit at the intersection of macro and structural themes: they benefit both from cyclical recoveries in PCs, smartphones, and autos and from structural AI‑driven data‑center demand.

Financials’ relative strength is also tied to the macro environment.
With credit performance remaining manageable and funding markets orderly, the major banks and card issuers have not seen the type of stress that would typically accompany a sharp macro downturn.
The modest steepening in investor expectations for the yield curve, coupled with an improved outlook for capital markets and deal activity, provides a supportive backdrop for bank net interest income and fee income.
This explains why names like Bank of America, Wells Fargo, JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Capital One, and Synchrony all delivered solid weekly and monthly gains.

In energy and materials, the macro narrative is one of balancing global growth expectations with supply dynamics and the energy transition.
The strong performance of copper‑levered Freeport‑McMoRan, steel producer Nucor, and aluminum player Kaiser Aluminum suggests that investors expect ongoing demand for industrial metals tied to infrastructure, grid upgrades, and data‑center construction.
At the same time, the more subdued performance of certain fertilizers and chemicals indicates that not all commodities are participating equally.
For portfolio construction, this means that targeted exposures to metals with clear demand drivers may be more attractive than broad, undifferentiated materials exposure.

## Watchlist Deep Dives

### Semiconductors: ALAB, INTC, MRVL, AVGO, SNDK, SITM, ONTO, TER, MU, TSM, LITE, POET, VRT

Astera Labs (ALAB) was the standout performer in our semiconductor cohort, rising 27.2% over the week and 19.5% over the month.
Astera sits directly in the AI‑heavy connectivity layer, providing high‑speed interconnect solutions for data‑center and AI infrastructure.
The magnitude of the move suggests that investors are increasingly appreciating the company’s leverage to AI server content per unit, as well as the potential for design wins at leading cloud customers.
The stock’s momentum, however, also introduces the risk that expectations for revenue growth and margin expansion get ahead of what the near‑term execution can deliver, making position sizing critical.

Intel (INTC) advanced 23.8% for the week and 30.0% over the month, a significant re‑rating for a company that has spent several years in transition.
The rally likely reflects a combination of factors: growing confidence in Intel’s foundry ambitions, improving sentiment around its CPU and accelerator roadmaps, and the perception that the company may be closer to trough profitability in legacy segments.
The sharp move also suggests a degree of short‑covering as investors who had underweighted Intel relative to AI leaders such as Nvidia and AMD reassess the risk of being structurally underexposed.
We continue to see Intel as a complex, multi‑year turnaround story where execution on process technology, foundry customer traction, and capital intensity will be critical swing factors.

Marvell Technology (MRVL) climbed 20.0% for the week and an impressive 42.1% over the month.
Marvell’s exposure to cloud and carrier infrastructure, particularly in custom silicon and optical connectivity, makes it a direct beneficiary of AI and data‑center build‑outs.
The stock’s trajectory suggests that investors are increasingly comfortable underwriting a multi‑year growth story driven by content gains in AI accelerators and networking, despite the inherent cyclicality of semis.
Valuation has expanded along with expectations, so any hiccups in hyperscaler capex or design cycles could introduce volatility, but the structural thesis remains intact.

Broadcom (AVGO) gained 18.1% weekly and 8.8% over the month, underscoring its role as both an AI infrastructure enabler and a diversified provider of networking, storage, and software assets.
The company’s custom AI accelerators and networking chips position it well as hyperscalers seek alternatives and complements to off‑the‑shelf GPUs.
Broadcom’s software portfolio also provides a stabilizing cash‑flow base, which investors value in the current environment.
While the stock’s absolute level has risen substantially over the past year, the recent week’s move indicates that investors continue to see upside as AI content per server expands.

Sandisk (SNDK) advanced 21.4% weekly and 30.0% monthly, while Seagate (STX) and Western Digital (WDC) gained 17.2% and 16.4% weekly and 30.4% and 27.8% monthly respectively.
These storage names are leveraged to both cyclical improvements in enterprise and cloud storage demand and secular growth in data generated and stored.
The coordinated move suggests that investors now view the storage cycle as having turned a corner, with excess inventory cleared and pricing stabilizing or improving.
For long‑term holders, these stocks offer leveraged exposure to data‑center capex and, by extension, to AI‑driven storage demand.

SiTime (SITM) rose 21.1% for the week and 19.8% over the month, highlighting investor enthusiasm for niche analog and timing components that are essential to high‑performance systems.
The company’s precision timing solutions are used across communications, data‑center, and industrial applications, and the market is recognizing the importance of such components in advanced electronics.
Onto Innovation (ONTO) gained 19.3% weekly and 33.4% monthly, reflecting strong demand for process control and metrology tools in advanced semiconductor manufacturing.
Teradyne (TER), up 18.9% for the week and 21.9% for the month, similarly benefits from increased test intensity in advanced ICs, particularly for AI and high‑performance computing chips.

Micron (MU) gained 14.8% for the week and is modestly positive for the month, adding to the broader memory‑and‑storage rally.
As a major high‑bandwidth memory supplier, Micron is firmly leveraged to AI workloads, and recent pricing trends have supported the view that the DRAM and NAND cycles are in recovery.
Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM) advanced 9.3% weekly and 4.5% monthly, continuing to serve as a bellwether for leading‑edge foundry demand.
Lumentum (LITE) gained 8.5% for the week and 33.5% over the month, benefiting from demand for optical components in data‑center and telecom networks, while POET Technologies (POET) advanced 15.2% weekly despite a modest monthly decline, reflecting its higher‑beta positioning within optoelectronics.
Vertiv (VRT), though technically a diversified infrastructure provider rather than a pure semi, gained 12.9% weekly and 10.0% monthly and is essential to the AI story via power and thermal management for data centers.

### Cloud & Software Infrastructure: FSLY, AKAM, NET, SNOW, IOT, DOCN, NTNX

Fastly (FSLY) endured the sharpest drawdown in our software infrastructure universe, declining 31.1% for the week and 4.1% over the month.
This move likely reflects mounting concerns about the company’s path to consistent profitability and its competitive positioning in a crowded content‑delivery and edge‑compute market.
The stock’s high beta and prior strong runs make it particularly vulnerable when investor appetite for unprofitable growth wanes.
Absent new company‑specific catalysts this week, the magnitude of the decline likely overshoots any incremental change in fundamentals, but it does underscore the need for clear evidence of operating leverage and differentiated product capabilities in coming quarters.

Akamai (AKAM) declined 22.6% weekly and 14.2% monthly, reinforcing the market’s skepticism toward the broader edge and security segment this week.
Akamai possesses a long‑standing content‑delivery network and a growing security business, with a more mature profitability profile than some peers.
However, the stock’s pullback suggests concerns that the growth profile may lag more pure‑play cloud security peers and that pricing competition in content delivery remains intense.
For value‑oriented investors, the drawdown may create an opportunity, provided one is comfortable with a more modest top‑line growth trajectory.

Cloudflare (NET) fell 21.1% for the week and 21.6% over the month.
Cloudflare had been priced as a premier high‑growth infrastructure platform, offering security, networking, and developer services on a unified edge platform.
The recent de‑rating reflects the market’s reduced tolerance for premium multiples, particularly for companies where near‑term free‑cash‑flow margins remain relatively thin compared with mature software peers.
Nevertheless, Cloudflare’s developer ecosystem and product velocity remain strategic assets, and the selloff should be evaluated against the company’s potential to drive AI‑related workloads and application services at the edge.

Snowflake (SNOW) lost 20.2% weekly and 32.5% monthly, marking a significant re‑rating.
As a central data‑platform provider, Snowflake is in the critical path for data warehousing and analytics, and increasingly for AI workloads.
The magnitude of the decline suggests that investors are re‑assessing the durability of elevated growth rates and the timing of margin expansion, particularly in light of increased competition from cloud providers and alternative data architectures.
For long‑term investors, the key question is whether the recent drawdown sufficiently compensates for these risks given Snowflake’s still‑strong net retention and product roadmap.

Samsara (IOT) declined 19.9% for the week and 19.4% for the month, reflecting a broader de‑rating in applied AI and IoT‑driven software.
Samsara’s platform connects physical assets and operations through sensors and analytics, an area with substantial long‑term potential.
However, as with many high‑growth software names, the stock is sensitive to any perceived slowdown in new logo additions or concerns about enterprise IT budget prioritization.
DigitalOcean (DOCN) fell 16.0% for the week but remains up 10.1% over the month, suggesting that while the name is not immune to software factor headwinds, there remains investor interest in its developer‑focused cloud niche.
Nutanix (NTNX) declined 16.3% weekly and 10.0% monthly, as investors likely revisit the competitive landscape in hybrid cloud and hyper‑converged infrastructure.

### Enterprise & Vertical Software: HUBS, NOW, INTU, TEAM, WDAY, ASAN, PCOR, MANH, BSY, PTC, ADSK, TYL, CSU.TO

HubSpot (HUBS) fell 21.4% over the week and 25.8% over the month, making it one of the most notable decliners in application software.
As a leading marketing and CRM platform for small and mid‑size businesses, HubSpot is tied to both marketing budgets and the health of smaller enterprises.
The sharp drawdown likely reflects a combination of valuation compression and concerns that customers may scrutinize marketing spend more closely if macro conditions become less favorable.
That said, the franchise remains strong, and for long‑term shareholders, the key question is whether the recent selloff creates a more attractive entry point relative to the company’s growth and profitability trajectory.

ServiceNow (NOW) declined 18.6% weekly and 28.2% monthly.
ServiceNow occupies a mission‑critical position in IT service management and increasingly in workflow automation across HR, customer service, and other functions.
The magnitude of the recent pullback suggests that even high‑quality, highly profitable software can be swept up in broad factor rotations.
Investors will be watching for evidence that AI‑enabled workflows can further expand the company’s addressable market and sustain growth, which could justify a re‑rating once the broader software selloff abates.

Intuit (INTU) lost 16.9% for the week and 20.3% for the month.
As a provider of tax preparation and small business accounting software, Intuit is tied to both consumer and SMB health.
The stock’s decline may reflect concerns about saturation in core categories, the competitive landscape in fintech‑adjacent solutions, and the valuation premium embedded in a mature, high‑margin franchise.
However, Intuit’s strong cash generation and ecosystem advantages remain intact, and the current weakness may ultimately prove cyclical rather than structural.

Atlassian (TEAM) fell 16.3% for the week and 24.2% over the month, while Workday (WDAY) declined 14.9% weekly and 18.4% monthly and Asana (ASAN) fell 14.3% weekly and 22.6% monthly.
These names each represent different aspects of productivity and HR software, but all share exposure to enterprise IT budgets and, in some cases, discretionary seat expansion.
The recent de‑rating reflects a combination of elevated starting valuations, questions around the pace of cloud seat growth, and investor concerns that generative AI could compress pricing for certain categories of collaboration and task‑management tools.
We believe the more mission‑critical platforms among them will ultimately find ways to embed AI to enhance user engagement and pricing power, but the market is demanding clearer evidence.

Procore (PCOR) declined 18.7% weekly and 15.9% monthly, highlighting pressure in industrial‑adjacent software tied to construction.
Manhattan Associates (MANH) fell 10.2% weekly and 15.7% monthly, while Bentley Systems (BSY) dropped 9.5% weekly and 19.0% monthly.
PTC declined 6.5% weekly and 16.1% monthly, and Autodesk (ADSK) fell 8.2% weekly and 13.2% monthly.
These vertical and industrial software players are crucial to infrastructure, manufacturing, and design workflows.
Their drawdowns may be partly attributable to concerns that project starts and industrial spending could slow if macro conditions deteriorate, alongside the broader software valuation reset.
Tyler Technologies (TYL), focused on public‑sector software, declined 6.1% weekly and 8.9% monthly, and Constellation Software (CSU.TO) fell 6.0% weekly and 15.0% monthly, indicating that even defensively perceived vertical software was not immune.

### Cybersecurity: OKTA, CRWD, ZS, S, QLYS, CHKP, TENB, VRNS, RPD

Okta (OKTA) was among the hardest hit security names, declining 21.5% for the week and 22.2% for the month.
Investors continue to scrutinize Okta’s ability to drive consistent growth in identity while managing competitive pressures from platform vendors.
The stock’s de‑rating reflects both execution questions and the broader market’s rotation away from high‑multiple software.
In our view, the underlying demand for identity and access management remains strong, but the company must demonstrate durable net retention and margin progress to regain investor confidence.

CrowdStrike (CRWD) declined 5.0% weekly and 14.2% monthly.
As a leading endpoint and XDR platform, CrowdStrike is more profitable and scaled than many peers, and its relative outperformance versus some other security names this week underscores that quality matters even in risk‑off tape.
However, the stock remains sensitive to any shifts in security budget prioritization and competitive intensity.
Zscaler (ZS), another high‑growth, high‑multiple security name, fell 14.8% weekly and 23.2% monthly, reflecting similar concerns around valuation and competition as secure access service edge architectures mature.

SentinelOne (S) and Varonis (VRNS) each declined 10.4% for the week and about 15.7% and 16.2% for the month respectively.
Qualys (QLYS) fell 13.8% weekly and 21.2% monthly, Check Point (CHKP) and Tenable (TENB) each declined 8.8% weekly and double digits monthly, and Rapid7 (RPD) dropped 5.6% for the week and 27.8% over the month.
These moves, taken together, point to a broad reassessment of security valuations.
We expect that over time, platforms with strong recurring revenue, high net retention, and clear paths to or existing robust profitability will regain favor, while more marginal, point‑solution vendors face increasing pressure from platform consolidation.

### Hyperscalers & Internet: AMZN, GOOG, META, NFLX, SHOP, WIX, PINS

Amazon (AMZN) was a bright spot, gaining 13.6% over the week and 12.1% for the month.
The move reflects confidence in both the retail and AWS narratives.
On the retail side, margin improvements from logistics optimization and advertising continue to drive earnings leverage.
On the cloud side, investors are increasingly focused on AWS’s ability to monetize generative AI workloads and higher‑value services, even as cloud growth rates normalize after the pandemic‑era surge.

Alphabet (GOOG) gained 7.2% weekly and 2.4% monthly, while Meta Platforms (META) advanced 9.6% for the week despite a slight 3.8% decline over the month.
Both companies remain core holdings for investors seeking diversified AI exposure.
Alphabet’s investments in AI infrastructure and models, coupled with its dominant search and YouTube franchises, provide multiple monetization avenues.
Meta’s story centers on robust advertising demand, improving Reels monetization, and heavy but strategically important AI infrastructure investment.
The weekly gains for both names, in a week when many software names were under pressure, underscore their relative resilience.

Netflix (NFLX), while not listed among the most extreme movers, appears within the AdTech/Digital Media subsector, where it posted a 4.4% weekly gain.
The stock benefits from subscription resilience and growing advertising initiatives.
In contrast, Shopify (SHOP) declined 6.3% weekly and 14.5% monthly, and Wix (WIX) dropped 20.5% weekly and 27.6% monthly, reflecting concerns about e‑commerce growth normalization and competition in website and commerce platforms.
Pinterest (PINS) declined 3.1% weekly, suggesting some relative resilience versus other ad‑tech names but still reflecting broader caution around consumer advertising.

### Fintech & Financials: BILL, LPLA, BAC, WFC, JPM, MS, GS, COF, SYF

BILL Holdings (BILL) declined 10.2% for the week and 15.8% for the month, highlighting pressure on mid‑cap fintech.
As a payments and back‑office automation platform geared to SMBs, BILL is sensitive to small‑business formation, churn, and spend.
The stock’s drawdown reflects concerns about competition and the potential for slower payment‑volume growth in a more cautious macro environment.
Investors will look for management to demonstrate durable monetization and cost discipline to re‑establish confidence.

At the other end of the spectrum, LPL Financial (LPLA) gained 6.4% for the week and 3.2% for the month, Bank of America (BAC) rose 6.4% weekly and 8.3% monthly, Wells Fargo (WFC) advanced 6.0% weekly and 11.1% monthly, and JPMorgan (JPM) gained 5.2% weekly and 7.8% monthly.
These moves underscore the resilience of large banks and wealth platforms in the current environment.
Morgan Stanley (MS) advanced 7.1% for the week and 10.4% for the month, Goldman Sachs (GS) gained 5.2% weekly and 10.2% monthly, Capital One (COF) climbed 6.1% weekly and 6.0% monthly, and Synchrony (SYF) rose 5.8% weekly and 11.0% monthly.
Collectively, this cohort’s performance suggests that investor anxiety about credit quality and capital‑markets activity has eased from prior peaks.

### Consumer & Staples: PVH, MKC, STZ, FIVE, UL, KDP, SHOP, WIX

PVH (PVH) delivered one of the strongest performances across the watchlist, rising 17.7% over the week and 48.7% for the month.
Such a move in an apparel name typically reflects strong execution on product, inventory, and brand strategy, as well as positive earnings or guidance catalysts in recent weeks.
The stock’s rally suggests that investors are differentiating within discretionary, rewarding companies that can navigate promotional environments while protecting margin.
It also indicates a willingness to own cyclical consumer names selectively, even amid mixed macro signals.

In consumer staples, McCormick (MKC) and Constellation Brands (STZ) both gained 9.9% weekly, with McCormick still down 10.4% for the month and Constellation up 10.8% for the month.
Unilever (UL) rose 5.2% weekly despite a 10.4% monthly decline, and Keurig Dr Pepper (KDP) gained 5.0% over the week.
These moves confirm that staples continue to serve as a ballast within portfolios, offering steady cash flows and, in some cases, pricing power.
Five Below (FIVE), in contrast, declined 7.7% for the week and is modestly down 0.5% for the month, and Shopify (SHOP) and Wix (WIX) saw meaningful declines as noted earlier.
This divergence underscores the need for careful stock selection within consumer, with a focus on balance sheet strength, brand power, and execution.

### Industrials, Energy & Materials: GLW, FIX, FCX, GEV, CAT, CNH, KALU, NUE, GNRC, BWXT, VMI, SOC, OXY, DVN, FCX, NEM

Corning (GLW) gained 15.8% weekly and 30.0% monthly, reflecting its unique positioning at the intersection of communications, display, and specialty materials.
The stock’s performance suggests rising confidence in demand for optical fiber and related products tied to data‑center and network build‑outs.
Comfort Systems USA (FIX), which gained 12.4% weekly and 13.2% monthly, is leveraged to mechanical and HVAC contracting, including data‑center and commercial projects.
Its strong performance highlights investors’ enthusiasm for companies that provide picks‑and‑shovels exposure to AI‑driven infrastructure investment.

Freeport‑McMoRan (FCX) gained 10.5% weekly and 10.2% monthly, underscoring its leverage to copper demand from electrification and infrastructure.
GE Vernova (GEV) rose 10.3% weekly and 16.9% monthly, Caterpillar (CAT) gained 10.2% weekly and 11.7% monthly, and CNH Industrial (CNH) advanced 8.6% weekly and 5.4% monthly.
Kaiser Aluminum (KALU) gained 8.4% weekly and 11.8% monthly, Nucor (NUE) advanced 7.9% weekly and 8.3% monthly, and Valmont (VMI) rose 5.7% weekly while modestly negative over the month.
These moves highlight that industrial and materials names tied to infrastructure, grid, and transportation investment are in favor, particularly those with exposure to structural trends like electrification and data‑center expansion.

Generac (GNRC) gained 6.7% weekly despite a slight monthly decline, and BWX Technologies (BWXT) rose 6.8% weekly and 17.1% monthly.
Generac benefits from backup power and energy resilience themes, while BWXT provides nuclear components and services, aligned with the growing interest in nuclear as a low‑carbon baseload energy source.
Sable Offshore (SOC) declined 14.5% weekly and 20.8% monthly, highlighting that not all energy names are participating equally; exploration and production names such as Occidental (OXY) and Devon (DVN) saw more modest weekly pressure, with Oxy down 7.9% weekly but positive over the month and Devon not listed among the most extreme moves.
Newmont (NEM), a major gold producer, gained 6.0% weekly and 4.0% monthly, suggesting that investors still value some exposure to precious metals as a portfolio diversifier.

## Upcoming Catalysts

Over the next two weeks, there are no earnings releases scheduled among the names on our watchlist, which shifts the focus toward macro data, policy communications, and sector‑specific news flow.
In the absence of company‑specific quarterly prints, investor attention will likely center on macro releases that inform the trajectory of inflation and growth, as well as any changes in central‑bank rhetoric.
For our watchlist, this means that factor and thematic dynamics are likely to dominate pricing in the near term, with continued potential for exaggerated moves in whichever direction flows are strongest.

Within technology and semiconductors, upcoming industry conferences, product announcements, and AI‑related events will be important catalysts.
Any incremental color from major hyperscalers and GPU vendors on AI infrastructure demand could further influence the trajectory of names like Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Marvell, Intel, Astera Labs, and key equipment and infrastructure players such as Onto Innovation, Teradyne, Taiwan Semiconductor, Vertiv, Arista, and Corning.
Similarly, commentary from large software vendors at industry events on AI monetization, seat growth, and pricing could shape sentiment toward application software and cloud infrastructure after this week’s drawdown.

For financials, catalysts will come from macro prints that affect rate expectations and credit conditions.
Stronger‑than‑expected growth or sticky inflation could influence the expected path of policy and hence bank net interest margins, while any signs of credit deterioration in consumer or commercial portfolios would resonate through names like Bank of America, JPMorgan, Wells Fargo, Capital One, and Synchrony.
Capital‑markets activity, including equity issuance and M&A announcements, will also matter for Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and LPL.

In consumer and staples, upcoming retail sales data and consumer‑confidence indicators will be watched for signals on discretionary spending.
Apparel and specialty retailers like PVH and Five Below are sensitive to shifts in consumer demand and promotional intensity.
E‑commerce and digital platforms like Shopify and Wix will respond to indications of online spending trends, while staples like McCormick, Constellation Brands, Unilever, and Keurig Dr Pepper will be more influenced by input‑cost dynamics and pricing power commentary from peers.

Energy, industrials, and materials will take their cues from commodity‑price trends, industrial production data, and policy developments related to infrastructure and energy transition.
Names like Freeport‑McMoRan, Nucor, Kaiser Aluminum, GE Vernova, Caterpillar, CNH Industrial, Valmont, Generac, and BWX Technologies will be particularly sensitive to signals about infrastructure and power‑grid investment.
Any announcements regarding new data‑center projects or large‑scale AI infrastructure investments could further support the thesis for data‑center exposed names like Vertiv, Comfort Systems USA, Corning, Arista, and related suppliers.

## What To Watch Next Week

For the coming week, we recommend focusing on several key themes that cut across our watchlist.
First, monitor whether the sharp rotation from software to semis and cyclicals extends, stabilizes, or partially reverses.
If semiconductors and AI infrastructure names such as Astera Labs, Intel, Marvell, Broadcom, Sandisk, Seagate, Western Digital, SiTime, Onto Innovation, Teradyne, Micron, Taiwan Semiconductor, Lumentum, and Vertiv continue to outperform after such robust weekly and monthly gains, it will reinforce the narrative that the AI hardware cycle remains in a powerful uptrend.
Conversely, any pause or reversal would suggest that a significant portion of near‑term optimism has already been priced in and that investors are rotating to laggards.

Second, watch for signs of stabilization in software and cybersecurity.
Names like HubSpot, ServiceNow, Intuit, Atlassian, Workday, Asana, Guidewire, Procore, Manhattan Associates, Bentley, PTC, Autodesk, Tyler, and Constellation Software have all experienced notable de‑ratings.
If these stocks can find a floor and begin to trade sideways or higher on neutral or modestly positive news, it would indicate that valuation risk has been partially absorbed and that the market is willing to look through near‑term factor headwinds.
Cybersecurity names such as Okta, CrowdStrike, Zscaler, SentinelOne, Varonis, Qualys, Check Point, Tenable, and Rapid7 will also be important tells; renewed interest in these names would signal a re‑embrace of secular security themes after a period of risk reduction.

Third, pay close attention to the behavior of hyperscalers and mega‑cap platforms.
Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, and to a lesser extent Netflix and Pinterest, remain central vehicles for exposure to AI and digital advertising.
Their comparatively strong weekly performance versus mid‑cap software suggests that they are acting as relative havens within growth.
If this dynamic persists, portfolio construction may favor concentrated positions in these names as core holdings, complemented by carefully selected higher‑beta satellite positions in semis, infrastructure, and software.
On the other hand, any broad weakness in these mega‑caps would likely signal a more generalized risk‑off move, which could spill over into the entire growth complex.

Fourth, track the resilience of financials.
Bank of America, Wells Fargo, JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Capital One, Synchrony, and LPL have all delivered solid weekly and monthly gains, supported by a benign credit backdrop and improving capital‑markets conditions.
If they continue to trade well, it will reinforce the view that the financial system is on stable footing and that investors remain comfortable with the earnings power of large banks and brokers.
Any sudden weakness or negative news flow on credit or regulation would warrant a re‑assessment of risk in these names and, by extension, in the broader market.

Finally, watch the interplay between real‑asset and cyclical exposures and the rest of the portfolio.
Industrial and materials names like Freeport‑McMoRan, Nucor, Kaiser Aluminum, Newmont, Corning, Comfort Systems USA, GE Vernova, Caterpillar, CNH Industrial, Valmont, Generac, and BWX Technologies have been relative winners.
Their continued outperformance would suggest that investors are positioning for sustained infrastructure, electrification, and data‑center investment.
If they begin to lag, it could indicate either profit‑taking after strong runs or a reassessment of the pace of these secular themes.
In either case, maintaining a diversified exposure to both secular growth and tangible‑asset beneficiaries remains prudent.

## Conclusion

This week underscored how quickly leadership can shift within growth and how violently factor rotations can play out when valuations are extended and positioning is crowded.
Semiconductors, AI infrastructure, financials, and select industrials and staples led decisively, with weekly gains often in the high single digits to mid‑twenties percent and substantial monthly outperformance.
Conversely, cloud infrastructure, application software, and cybersecurity experienced sharp drawdowns, with many names down mid‑teens to low‑twenties percent on the week and even more over the month.
Yet, beneath this volatility, the underlying secular themes—AI, data‑center expansion, digital transformation, security, and electrification—remain intact.

For buy‑side portfolios, the near‑term playbook should emphasize three principles.
First, lean into quality within all sectors, favoring companies with strong balance sheets, clear competitive moats, and visible paths to sustainable cash‑flow growth.
Second, use volatility and factor‑driven dislocations to upgrade portfolios, rotating from names where valuation still discounts a near‑perfect scenario into those where recent selloffs have reset expectations to more achievable levels.
Third, maintain diversification across AI hardware, AI‑enabled software, financials, and real‑asset beneficiaries to avoid over‑concentration in any single thematic or factor exposure.

Looking ahead to the coming weeks, absent watchlist earnings, macro data and narrative will drive cross‑asset sentiment, while sector‑specific news and industry events will shape relative performance within technology, financials, consumer, industrials, and materials.
Investors should be prepared for continued high dispersion and remain nimble in adjusting exposures as new information emerges.
The current environment rewards those who can distinguish between short‑term factor noise and genuine shifts in fundamental trajectories, and who are willing to take the other side of crowded trades when the risk‑reward becomes compelling.
In that context, this week’s rotation offers both a warning about the risks of complacency in richly valued segments and an opportunity to position portfolios for the next leg of secular growth across AI, infrastructure, and high‑quality cash‑generative franchises.
